en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Section on the Puzzles,
Chapter on Intimacy.
5. The Question on Not Harassing Beings “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Formerly, when I was a human being, I was by nature one who did not harass living beings.’”
But it is also said:
‘The seer named Lomasakassapa, while being a seer, sacrificed a great Vājapeyya offering after having caused the slaughter of many hundreds of living beings.
If, venerable Nāgasena, it was said by the Blessed One—
‘In the past, when I was a human being, I was by nature one who did not harm living beings’— if that is so, then the statement that “the seer Lomasakassapa,
having caused the slaughter of many hundreds of living beings, performed the Vājapeyya great sacrifice” is false. If indeed “the seer Lomasakassapa,
having caused the slaughter of many hundreds of living beings, performed the Vājapeyya great sacrifice,” [then my claim is proven].
"In that case, the statement: 'In the past, when I was a human being, I was by nature one who did not harm living beings'—that too is false.
This question, which has two sides, has now come to you; it must be resolved by you.
"Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:"
‘In the past, when I was a human being, I was by nature one who did not harm living beings,’ yet ‘the seer Lomasakassapa,
having caused the slaughter of many hundreds of creatures, performed the Vājapeyya great sacrifice’— and that was done out of lust, by one whose mind was deranged,
not by one who was conscious.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, there are these eight kinds of persons who take life. Which eight?
One who is lustful takes life through the power of lust; one who is hateful takes life through the power of hatred; one who is deluded takes life through the power of delusion...”
He kills: the proud man kills out of pride; the greedy man kills out of greed; the destitute man kills for the sake of a livelihood;
the fool kills out of merriment; and the king kills for the sake of discipline.
These, venerable Nāgasena, are the eight types of persons who kill living beings.
“It was merely natural, venerable Nāgasena, that the Bodhisatta did this.

“No, Great King, it was not merely natural that the Bodhisatta did this. For if, Great King, the Bodhisatta had bowed down in his ordinary state to perform the great sacrifice, he would not have spoken this verse:
‘The earth, together with its ocean boundaries...’”
One should not desire the earth with its earrings of oceans together with blame;
thus should it be understood by one who knows.
"Thus it was said, O Great King: upon seeing Princess Candavatī, the Bodhisatta became senseless, his mind distracted, impassioned, and utterly bewildered;
agitated and frantic with that scattered, wandering, and turbid mind, he performed the great Vājapeyya sacrifice, which involved a vast heap of the blood from the throats of slaughtered animals."
Just as, O Great King, a madman with a deranged mind steps upon blazing fire, seizes a provoked venomous snake,
approaches a rutting elephant, leaps into a shoreless ocean, tramples in a cesspool or a puddle of filth,
climbs onto a bed of thorns, falls over a precipice, and eats impure things; so too, O Great King, does one who is obsessed by sensual desire act.
Even when naked, he wanders the streets and performs many other kinds of improper acts.

In the same way, Great King, as soon as the Bodhisatta saw the princess Candavatī, he became senseless, his mind distracted, impassioned, utterly bewildered, agitated, and frantic; with his mind thus scattered, wandering, and turbid—
"He performed the Vājapeyya great sacrifice, which involved a vast heap of the blood from the throats of many slaughtered animals.
Great King, an evil deed committed by one whose mind is deranged is not considered a grave offense even in this present life, nor does it bear such a result in the future life.
Great King, if some madman here were to commit a crime punishable by death, what punishment would you impose upon him?"
“Venerable sir, what punishment will there be for a madman? We shall have him beaten and driven out; that itself is his punishment.
“In this way, great king, there is no punishment for the offense of a madman; therefore, even if something is done by a madman, it is not a fault, as it can be remedied.
In the same way, great king, the seer Lomasakassapa lost consciousness upon merely seeing the royal maiden Candavatī.”
"He became deranged, impassioned, unconscious, distracted, agitated, overwhelmed, and frantic;
with that mind scattered, wandering, and whirling, he performed the Vājapeyya great sacrifice, a heap of blood from the throats of many hundreds of slaughtered animals.
But when his mind returned to its natural state and he regained his mindfulness, he went forth once again, realized the five super-knowledges (pañca-abhiññā), and was reborn in the Brahma-world."
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
This is the fifth question, on not harassing the Buddha.
